newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Gonzalez awaits "dirty war" court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Gonzalez awaits "dirty war" court ruling.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court will decide on Monday whether to question former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, either as a witness or as a suspect, in a probe of a "dirty war" against Basque separatists in the 1980s.

Former security chiefs and a disgruntled Socialist leader have accused Gonzalez of masterminding a campaign of killing, torture and kidnapping between 1983 and 1987 in which 28 people were murdered, a third of them in error.

Supreme Court justice Eduardo Moner ruled earlier this year that there was insufficient evidence to investigate Gonzalez and two other top Socialists. He subsequently refused to consider any appeal, arguing that it was not legally admissible.
But the Supreme Court over-ruled his decision and accepted an appeal by families of the victims in September.

Newspapers on Sunday printed detailed biographies of the 10 Supreme Court justices who will decide on Monday whether to question Gonzalez, his former deputy Narcis Serra and Jose Maria Benegas, a Socialist member of parliament.

Pro-conservative daily El Mundo on Sunday published extracts from a new book alleging that Benegas tried to bribe policemen convicted in the dirty war scandal to keep them from testifying against top Socialist officials.

The Spanish media speculated that some judges' sympathy for the Socialists could create internal divisions, added that the recommendation of state attorney Juan Cesareo Ortiz Urculo, although not binding, could be a deciding factor.
Urculo is expected to support the opinion of an advisory committee of top judges which decided unanimously this week that sufficient grounds did not exist to question Gonzalez.
Failure to call him to testify would bring shame not only on the judges but also on the conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, the newspaper El Mundo said in an editorial.

"A big part of the blame for creating a social climate which gives rise to these symptoms (of ignoring new evidence) can be laid at the door of Aznar's government for not declassifying the CESID (secret service) papers," the paper said.

Aznar, who used the dirty war charges to help achieve a narrow defeat of Gonzalez at a general election last March, has subsequently refused court requests to declassify military files on the anti-ETA campaign, saying it was up to judges to resolve the issue.

But his number two, Francisco Alvarez Cascos, accused Gonzalez in September of having waged "bodeguilla terrorism" from a wine cellar in his official residence where he entertained friends and hatched strategies with his aides.
Alvarez Cascos is in charge of Spain's secret services and has unrivalled access to top-secret information.
Attorneys defending an anti-terrorist police chief in a case linked to the dirty war subsequently called on Alvarez Cascos to testify, but the Supreme Court has yet to study the petition.
The court is the only authority in Spain which can decide whether current members of parliament should be questioned, either as witnesses or as suspects, in criminal cases.

Gonzalez has always denied any knowledge of the activities of the GAL (Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups), death squads made up of security forces and hired gunmen who waged the illegal campaign against Basque separatists.
ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) has killed around 800 people since 1968 in its drive for an independent Basque state.
Gonzalez's former interior minister Jose Barrionuevo is already on trial before the Supreme Court on charges of creating and funding the GAL.
